Dube, 43, was killed in Johannesburg around 8 p.m. local time Thursday after someone tried to steal his car, Gallo Record Company said in a statement. Police said he was shot. The statement said Dube attempted to escape but died almost instantly from his wounds. Dube was much loved by his fellow South Africans, and his death cast a shadow over festivities ahead of South Africa's highly-anticipated appearance in the rugby World Cup final with England this weekend. News of his death was the headline in many Friday newspapers, knocking the World Cup off the front pages for the first time in days. Callers to talk radio stations suggested the Springboks wear black armbands in remembrance of Dube when they take to the field Saturday in Paris. (He was) one of their most successful artists and certainly one of their leading reggae artists." Sutherland said Dube was an extremely respected musician who toured extensively around the world. Dube had just returned from a tour of the United States that stretched from California to New York. His record company said Dube leaves "a great void" in the music industry after a 25-year career. Dube recorded 22 albums in Zulu, English and Afrikaans. Born outside Johannesburg in 1964, Dube was named "Lucky" by his mother because he was the first child to be born after several failed pregnancies. Dube started singing in 1982, joining a band playing Mbaqanga, or traditional Zulu music. It was only later that he began recording reggae tracks as a solo singer, but the genre was to dominate and define the remainder of his career. Ivor Haarburger, the chief exectutive of Gallo Music Group, said he was deeply saddened by the loss. "Lucky was not just an extraordinary artist, he was a personal friend," Haarburger said. "It's so sad to lose such a great friend and so tragically." **Lucky Dube, South African Reggae Star, Killed in Johannesburg**

Lucky Dube, the South African reggae singer whose powerful songs about apartheid, faith, exile, and social justice made him one of Africa’s most internationally recognized musicians, was shot dead in Johannesburg on Thursday night in an apparent attempted carjacking. He was 43.

Police said Dube was killed in the suburb of Rosettenville shortly after dropping off, or preparing to drop off, members of his family. According to early reports, his attackers opened fire as he was driving, in what authorities described as a botched hijacking. His children were reportedly nearby or in the vehicle at the time of the shooting, adding to the shock that spread quickly through South Africa and the global music community.

His record company, Gallo Records, issued a statement expressing deep grief at the killing, calling Dube not only one of the label’s most important artists but a national and continental treasure. The company said it was devastated by the loss of a musician whose voice had carried South African reggae onto the world stage and whose work had touched audiences across race, class, and national borders.

Dube’s death came at a moment when South Africa was otherwise absorbed in celebration and anticipation. The country’s Springboks were preparing for the Rugby World Cup final against England in Paris, a match that had stirred memories of the unifying 1995 World Cup victory under Nelson Mandela. But the killing of one of the nation’s best-loved performers sharply interrupted the mood of sporting pride, forcing South Africans once again to confront the violent crime that has shadowed public life in the post-apartheid era.

Born Lucky Philip Dube on August 3, 1964, in Ermelo, in what is now Mpumalanga province, he was raised largely by his grandmother. His mother reportedly named him “Lucky” because she considered his birth fortunate after earlier difficulties having children. He began performing while still young, first drawn to traditional Zulu music and mbaqanga before turning to reggae — a genre he embraced for its spiritual force and its language of resistance.

Dube rose to prominence in the 1980s and 1990s with a string of albums that made him a household name in South Africa and a major figure in international reggae. Though he was often compared to Jamaican reggae icons, he developed a distinctly South African voice, blending roots reggae rhythms with themes drawn from apartheid, township life, displacement, political oppression, and the search for dignity.

Albums such as **“Slave,” “Prisoner,” “Captured Live,” “House of Exile,” “Victims,” “Trinity,” “The Way It Is,”** and **“Respect”** brought him critical acclaim and a devoted following across Africa, Europe, the Caribbean, and beyond. His songs — including **“Prisoner,” “Together as One,” “Slave,” “Remember Me,” “House of Exile,”** and **“Different Colours / One People”** — became anthems for listeners confronting injustice and inequality.

At a time when apartheid still governed South Africa, Dube’s music spoke directly to division and repression. Yet his songs often reached beyond politics into family, faith, personal responsibility, and moral struggle. He sang against racism, violence, corruption, and broken homes, but also insisted on unity and hope. His 1988 song **“Together as One”** was among the first widely known South African reggae songs to openly call for racial unity during apartheid.

Dube was also admired for his stagecraft: tall, dreadlocked, and commanding, he performed with intensity and warmth, helping make reggae a major force in South African popular music. He toured widely and won numerous awards, becoming one of the continent’s best-selling reggae artists. His success demonstrated that reggae, though born in Jamaica, could be reshaped through African experiences and languages into a vehicle for local and global protest.

News of his murder brought tributes from fellow musicians, fans, broadcasters, and political figures. Many described his death as an unbearable irony: an artist who had spent his life singing against violence had become a victim of it. Others pointed to the killing as another sign of South Africa’s struggle with armed crime, particularly vehicle hijackings, which had become a source of fear in major cities.

Dube’s death left a profound gap in African music. He was more than a reggae singer; he was a cultural bridge between township South Africa and the wider world, between the liberation era and the uncertain freedoms that followed. His songs gave voice to the oppressed while refusing despair, and his message of unity remained central to his art.

He is survived by his children and family, and by a body of work that continues to resonate across generations. For millions of listeners, Lucky Dube’s voice remains inseparable from the promise that people of “different colours” might still live as one.
